source_refs.note: Topic 30.7.2 with Quick Check 30.6, answered (PDF 213); the ethanol spectrum (printed as 'Figure 30.3', i.e. Figure 30.7) is redrawn. The 1.1% note is added to explain lower sensitivity. Answers need review.

blocks.text: A 13C NMR spectrum is simpler than a 1H spectrum: each peak corresponds to one different environment (type) of carbon atom, and its chemical shift tells which environment. The number of peaks equals the number of different carbon environments. Ethane gives one peak, because both carbons are in the same environment. Propane, CH3-CH2-CH3, has two environments, the two equivalent terminal CH3 carbons and the middle CH2 carbon, so it gives two peaks. Ethanol, CH3-CH2-OH, also gives two peaks: by Table 30.3 the peak at 18 ppm is the CH3 carbon and the peak near 57 ppm is the CH2 carbon attached to oxygen.

13C and 1H spectra differ in two key ways. In 13C NMR the relative peak area is usually not proportional to the number of carbon atoms, unlike 1H NMR, where the peak area shows the number of protons. The 13C peaks also do not show splitting, so they appear as single vertical lines. (The book adds that 13C NMR is less sensitive than 1H NMR; this is mainly because only about 1.1% of carbon atoms are 13C.)

blocks.alt: Top: horizontal bars on a 220 to 0 ppm scale for the 13C shift ranges of Table 30.3, from C=O of aldehydes and ketones (190-220) to alkyl carbon (0-50). Bottom left: a sketch of the 13C spectrum of ethanol, lines at 57 ppm (CH2) and 18 ppm (CH3). Bottom right: the three lines of Figure 30.8 at 69.0, 30.5 and 19.0 ppm.
blocks.caption: 13C chemical shift ranges, ethanol, and the unknown of Figure 30.8 (original diagram after Table 30.3 and Figures 30.7 and 30.8).
blocks.long_description: Each different carbon environment gives one unsplit line. Carbons bonded to oxygen appear at 50-70 ppm, and carbonyl carbons much further left. Counting the lines gives the number of carbon environments.

blocks.prompt: How many signals are expected in the 13C NMR spectrum of butane? Justify.
blocks.explanation: Two: CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3 is symmetrical, so the two CH3 carbons are equivalent and the two CH2 carbons are equivalent.

blocks.prompt: Predict the 13C NMR spectrum of butan-2-ol.
blocks.explanation: Four peaks, one for each carbon of CH3-CH(OH)-CH2-CH3: the C-O carbon at 50-70 ppm (about 69) and three alkyl carbons at 0-50 ppm (about 32, 23 and 10).

blocks.prompt: Predict the chemical shifts of the carbon atoms in propanoic acid.
blocks.explanation: CH3CH2COOH has three peaks: the COOH carbon at 160-185 ppm, the CH2 next to the carboxyl group in the 30-65 ppm range of Table 30.3 (about 28 ppm in practice) and the CH3 at 0-50 ppm (about 9 ppm).

items: Number of 13C peaks = number of carbon environments.
No splitting; areas not proportional to numbers of carbons.
